content: The Grahamites were followers of Reverend Sylvester Graham, a Presbyterian minister and dietary reformer who lived from 1794 to 1851. Graham advocated for a lifestyle that would now be considered part of alternative medicine, though such terminology did not exist during his time. His followers adhered strictly to his teachings, which encompassed all aspects of daily life. They practiced abstinence from alcohol, engaged in frequent bathing, followed a vegetarian diet, and embraced a generally austere way of living. Graham was a strong proponent of sexual abstinence, particularly opposing masturbation, which he believed was a moral evil that could lead to insanity. He also held the view that all forms of excitement were detrimental to health. Consequently, he prohibited the use of spices in food, which resulted in a diet that was notably bland. This dietary philosophy led to the creation and consumption of Graham crackers, a product he invented to align with his principles. Graham and his followers condemned white bread, arguing that it was nutritionally deficient—a claim that has been echoed by advocates of alternative medicine and nutritionists in subsequent years. Some of Graham's followers became disillusioned after his death at the age of 57. Despite this, the Grahamites made a lasting cultural impact, particularly through their emphasis on frequent bathing. This practice influenced American hygiene habits, and to this day, Americans are known for bathing more frequently than people in many other cultures. Another significant legacy of Graham's teachings can be seen in the work of Dr. John Harvey Kellogg and his brother Will Keith Kellogg, who were inspired by Graham's nutritional philosophy. Their invention of corn flakes was a natural progression of the Grahamite dietary principles. Grahamism also played a role in shaping the vegan movement. Graham believed that meat and dairy products were responsible for stimulating sexual desires, asserting that animal-derived foods incited lust. As a result, Grahamism rejected the consumption of meat, animal byproducts, and alcohol in pursuit of a purer mind and body. While the movement enjoyed popularity during the 1860s to 1880s, it eventually declined and is now primarily remembered for its association with Graham crackers.
